extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming, evaluating, and applying inductive generalizations (both universal and approximate), distinguishing laws of causation from mere empirical co‑existences and assessing strength of evidence and limits of application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uniformities of co-existence from causal succession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no general axiom standing in the same relation to uniformities of co-existence as the law of causation does to uniformities in succession; methods of elimination (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations) that work for causation are inapplicable to many co-existence questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply Baconian elimination indiscriminately to properties alleged to co-exist in kinds (e.g., hardness, color). The principle that every event has a cause underpins methods for succession but gives no analogue for co-existence; thus you cannot rely on invariable co-existent circumstances in the same way as invariable antecedents. Anti-pattern: trying to find an invariable co-existent 'form' for a property when none exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat co-existence generalizations as empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities of co-existence—even when apparently ultimate—are entitled to reception only as empirical laws and are amenable to the same rules as other unresolved derivative laws dependent on causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such generalizations lack the necessary certainty of laws of causation and must be held only within the limits (time, place, circumstance) of observation. Expect readiness to revise on new evidence; do not assume metaphysical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure certainty by improbability of an unobserved exception
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of certainty of a generalization resting solely on past observation is the degree of improbability that an exception, if any existed, could have so far remained unobserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recast 'All A are B' as 'How improbable is it that any non-B A has existed without detection?' Use this framing to assess strength of evidence. Example: believing 'All crows are black' is justified to the extent that white crows would be unlikely to have escaped notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether a property is causal (derivative) or an ultimate property of Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: If a property can vary within the same Kind (e.g., flower color), it is likely an effect of causes and thus the universality of the property indicates common causes; if it is truly a property of Kind, exceptions would indicate a previously unrecognized Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether variation within the Kind occurs and whether variation also occurs over time in same individuals. For organized beings variability suggests derivative properties. Example guidance: sulfur's color appears constant (suggesting ultimate property) while flower color varies (suggesting causal dependence).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit generalizations to the circumstances of observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical generalizations should be received only within the limits of time, place, and circumstance in which observations were made, with cautious extension only to strictly adjacent cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unqualified extension to different populations or settings. Be prepared to abandon the generalization on credible counterevidence from previously unexamined localities or circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require stronger evidence for overturning more general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: It requires much more evidence to establish an exception to a more general empirical law than to a more special one; the more general the law, the less probable an exception appears (though not impossible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess improbability of exception relative to the generality: finding a new Kind contradicting a very general law is harder to believe than contradicting a narrow law. Use degree of generality to weight skepticism toward reported novelties.

rubrics_metrics.name: When generalizing about superior Kinds, examine all included sub-kinds
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal propositions respecting properties of superior Kinds, unless grounded on causal connection, ought not to be made except after separately examining every known sub-kind (infimæ species) comprised by the larger Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not infer a property of a large class from a subset unless there is causal reason to do so. Where exhaustive examination is impractical, hold the generalization as provisional and subject to revision on discovery of counterexamples among sub-kinds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximate generalizations (Most A are B) are empirical and of lower certainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions of the form 'Most A are B' cannot be laws of causation or ultimate truths and possess lower certainty; they are either steps toward universal truths or practical guides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize their provisional character and use them primarily as intermediate conclusions or pragmatic rules when universals are unavailable. They can often be superseded by finer classifications that yield universal propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use approximate generalizations pragmatically when more precise info is unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice, especially under time constraints or complex cases (e.g., moral/predictive judgments about human action), one often must rely on 'Most A are B' to guide decisions despite their fallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate risk by seeking corroborating indications, combining multiple approximate generalizations, or—where possible—examining known causes or marks that distinguish members of the class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess sufficiency of evidence for approximate generalizations by scope and mode of knowing
rubrics_metrics.description: When 'Most A are B' is all we know, it rests on counting instances to eliminate chance and is only reliable within observed limits; when we also know causes or distinguishing marks, we can assess by checking frequency of causes or marks as well as effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer the indirect mode (examining causes/marks) when accessible because it can provide firmer grounds; combine direct incidence counts with causal/mark-based checks when possible (e.g., literacy: observed readers + school attendance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer identifying causes or marks over relying on raw approximations
rubrics_metrics.description: Wherever possible, replace an approximate generalization by a certain indication—i.e., recognizing the presence of a cause or mark that guarantees the attribute—because that yields greater reliability for particular cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: instead of relying on 'most people tell the truth', examine witness honesty, accuracy, or interest to serve; use collateral marks (reputation, past conduct) to improve assessment of an individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply numerical frequencies only to average cases and within observed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: If an empirical law states 'nine out of ten A are B,' you may treat an unknown A as B with 1-in-10 chance of error — but this holds only within limits of observation and only for average cases not known to belong to a particular sub-class or special circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply genus-level averages to instances known to be from a non-average sub-class. Averages inform decisions about large numbers (insurance) but are poor guides for particular, atypical individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine approximate generalizations with attention to modes of combination (addition vs deduction)
rubrics_metrics.description: When combining two approximate generalizations: (a) where each applies separately to the case (independent support), probabilities combine additively yielding a higher probability; (b) where one generalization is applied only by virtue of another (deductive chaining), the resulting probability is lower than either individual probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use additive combination when you have independent lines of evidence (e.g., two unconnected witnesses). Beware of chaining (e.g., hearsay), which compounds uncertainty and reduces reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge organismal variability implies causal derivation of properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Organized beings show high variability among individuals and over time, implying that their properties are likely derivative and produced by causes rather than ultimate properties of Kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dealing with living organisms, expect greater modifiability and seek causal explanations; avoid treating observed regularities among organisms as ultimate without causal investigation.
